summary: Specifies the syntax and processing rules for digital signatures on XML data. It is on the standards track. It was replaced by RFC 3275.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a way to sign a document written in XML so others can check it was not changed. A newer document later replaced it.

questions: what is the difference between enveloped and detached signatures
what is canonicalization in xml signatures
what is a manifest in xml signature
subtitle: Syntax and processing rules for digital signatures over XML and other data, wherever the data lives.

tldr.problem: There was no standard XML format for signing data, whether that data sits inside the same XML document as the signature or elsewhere.
tldr.mechanism: A Signature element holds a SignedInfo block listing the algorithms and, for each signed object, a Reference with its digest. The signature is computed over the canonicalized SignedInfo, so the digests are protected too.
tldr.outcome: It provides integrity, message authentication and signer authentication, but leaves open how keys map to people and what signed data means. RFC 3275 replaced this document.

facts.label: Version number
facts.value: None; a new version would use a new namespace

today: RFC 3075 was obsoleted by RFC 3275, which is the current version of this specification. Its status is Proposed Standard.

sections.title: What an XML Signature Is
sections.content:
An XML Signature can be applied to any digital content, including XML. Enveloped and enveloping signatures are over data in the same XML document as the signature; detached signatures are over data external to the signature element. The RFC defines the signature element type, plus types for referencing collections of resources, algorithms and key information.

It is a method of associating a key with referenced data. It does not say how keys are tied to persons or institutions, nor what the signed data means. An application that needs those things must specify its own key, algorithm, processing and rendering requirements.

No version number is carried in the syntax; a future version would use a different namespace. The namespace that implementations MUST use is http://www.w3.org/2000/09/xmldsig#.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a seal you can attach to any file, whether the seal goes inside the file, wraps around it, or sits next to it. It does not say who the signer really is, only which key made the seal.

sections.title: The Signature Element
sections.content:
The root element is Signature. It contains, in order, SignedInfo, SignatureValue, an optional KeyInfo and any number of Object elements. SignedInfo is the part that is actually signed. It holds a CanonicalizationMethod, a SignatureMethod and one or more Reference elements.

Each Reference names a data object with an optional URI, may list Transforms applied before digesting, and carries a DigestMethod and a DigestValue. The URI may be omitted on at most one Reference. The algorithm names sit inside SignedInfo so that an attacker cannot swap in a weaker algorithm.

KeyInfo tells the verifier which key to use. It is optional because the signer may not want to reveal key information to everyone, or the key may be known from context. Compliant implementations MUST implement KeyValue and SHOULD implement RetrievalMethod; other types include X509Data, PGPData and SPKIData. An Object element can carry the signed data itself, usually for enveloping signatures.
sections.plainLanguage: The seal has a list of the things it covers, with a fingerprint of each one. The seal is then stamped over that list, so changing any item or its fingerprint breaks it.

sections.title: Generating and Validating
sections.content:
To generate a signature, first make each Reference: apply the Transforms to the data object, digest the result and record the digest. Then build SignedInfo, canonicalize it, compute the SignatureValue over it, and assemble the Signature element.

Core validation has two required parts. Reference validation digests each referenced object and compares it with its DigestValue, and any mismatch fails validation. Signature validation gets the key from KeyInfo or an outside source and checks the SignatureValue over the canonical form of SignedInfo.

A verifier may get the data from somewhere other than the URI, such as a local cache, so long as the digest matches. The RFC notes that some valid signatures cannot be validated by some applications, for instance when they do not implement an optional part or will not dereference a URI that could cause side effects.
sections.plainLanguage: To check the seal, recompute the fingerprint of every item and compare it with the list, then check that the stamp over the list is genuine.

sections.title: Algorithms and Transforms
sections.content:
Algorithms are named by URIs. The required set is SHA-1 for digests, base64 for encoding, HMAC-SHA1 for MACs, DSA with SHA-1 for signatures, Canonical XML (without comments) for canonicalization, and the enveloped-signature transform. RSA with SHA-1, Canonical XML with Comments, minimal canonicalization and XPath are RECOMMENDED, and XSLT is OPTIONAL. User-defined algorithms are permitted. MD5 is NOT RECOMMENDED because advances in cryptography have cast doubt on its strength.

Canonicalization turns XML into a single standard byte form, so that harmless differences in text representation do not change the digest. Transforms are ordered steps applied before digesting, such as canonicalization, base64 decoding, XPath filtering or XSLT. The enveloped-signature transform removes the Signature element itself from the digest when the signature is inside the data it signs.
sections.plainLanguage: Before fingerprinting, the text is tidied into one standard form so that spacing differences do not matter. The RFC also lists which fingerprint and signing methods every program must support.

sections.title: Manifests and Signature Properties
sections.content:
A Manifest is a list of References kept outside SignedInfo, in an Object. SignedInfo references the Manifest instead. This lets an application decide for itself what a failed reference means: with plain References, one bad digest fails the whole signature, but with a Manifest the application controls reference validation. It also lets many Signature elements share one large list of references.

SignatureProperties carry statements about the signature itself, such as the time of signing, and can be signed by referencing them from SignedInfo. The RFC does not address making statements or assertions about the signed data; applications must use other technologies for that.
sections.plainLanguage: A manifest is a checklist of items that can be signed as one bundle, so you can decide what to do if one item is wrong. Properties are notes on the seal itself, like the time it was made.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Transforms raise three cautions. Only what is signed is secure, so anything a transform discards is not protected. Only what is "seen" should be signed, so if a signature conveys a user's consent, the data should include whatever affects how it was presented. And what is signed should be what is "seen": those who trust a signature should work from the transformed, signed data, and external resources such as a style sheet should also be signed via a Reference.

The security model also differs by algorithm. Public key signatures let anyone verify but only the private key holder sign, while keyed hash codes need every verifier to hold the same secret, so any verifier can forge signatures. Finally, a signature is only as strong as the whole chain: algorithms, key size, key generation, certificate validation and protection of processing. The RFC warns that perverse algorithm parameters might cause unacceptable processing or memory demand.
sections.plainLanguage: A seal only protects what it covers, so sign exactly what the reader sees, and remember that a shared secret lets anyone holding it forge the seal.
